title: Order Alerts and Weekly Offers
prompt: A food delivery app sends order status alerts by push, with a text message as a fallback, and a weekly offers email. Design the notification system, using the full routine.
facts: About 8 million users; about 15 million order status alerts a day, up to 2,000 per second at dinner time; the weekly offers email goes to about 6 million users, all in US time zones from Hawaii (UTC−10) to Eastern (UTC−5), and the batch starts at 10:00 Pacific time

Providers: push accepts 5,000 per second and reports within 2 minutes whether each push was delivered to the phone; SMS accepts 50 per second and costs money per message; email accepts 500 per second and an idempotency key, and drops a repeated request with the same key for 24 hours. Push and SMS have no idempotency key

Measured: about 1% of pushes are not delivered, and about half of those users allow SMS for order alerts; retries add at most 5% to the requests sent to any provider; a provider outage has lasted at most 1 hour
Order events arrive on a queue with at-least-once delivery, and an event is redelivered for at most 2 days; workers skip any event older than 2 days
Senders handle up to 10,000 messages per second, and a message waits under 1 second in its queue while its provider's quota is not full

The database accepts about 5,000 inserts per second under a unique key; an in-memory store runs about 100,000 "set if absent" operations per second, with a time limit per key, and acknowledges only after its replica has the change

Requirement: an order alert is handed to the push service within 30 seconds of the event. If the push is reported not delivered and the user allows SMS for order alerts at that moment, one SMS is attempted. A crash between claiming a push or an SMS and sending it may lose that message; this rare miss is accepted, and a duplicate is not: a user never gets the same order status twice through the same channel, and never an SMS when the push was delivered

Requirement: the offers email goes only to users who are opted in at the moment of sending, never during their quiet hours (22:00 to 8:00 local time), at most once per user, and every email is handed to the provider within 24 hours of the start
Requirement: no provider quota is ever exceeded, retries included
scope: Order alerts and the weekly offers email
Writing the message text and the offers themselves are out of scope

requirements: States push handed over within 30 seconds; one SMS attempt only when the push was reported not delivered and SMS is allowed; rare misses after a crash accepted, duplicates not; offers only to users opted in at send time, outside quiet hours, at most once, within 24 hours; quotas never exceeded
estimation: Order alerts: 2,000 per second × 1.05 for retries = 2,100, under push's 5,000 and the senders' 10,000; with under 1 second in the queue, a push is handed over well within 30 seconds; attempt-key inserts about 2,100 per second, under 5,000
SMS: about 2,000 × 1% × 50% = 10 per second expected at peak, under 50; a short burst above 50 waits in the SMS queue, which has no deadline

Offers: 6 million × 1.05 = 6.3 million requests ÷ 500 per second = 12,600 seconds, about 3.5 hours, plus at most 1 hour of outage, about 4.5 hours: from 10:00 Pacific time (13:00 Eastern, 8:00 in Hawaii) it ends by about 14:30 Pacific time, inside every user's 8:00 to 22:00 and well within 24 hours
design: API (notify from the order service), data model (preferences, quiet hours and time zone; a notification ID and one attempt per channel with its state), a high-level design with a queue per channel, senders with a pacer per provider, and a delayed fallback check, and a deep dive on deduplication across redelivery, retries and the fallback, and on preferences checked by the sender at each attempt
data: A notification ID (order, order status, user) and an attempt key (notification ID, channel), claimed before each send; the SMS attempt claimed only after a "not delivered" report; the email provider's key equal to the attempt key
Keys kept longer than the 2-day redelivery limit; preferences and quiet hours read by the sender just before each attempt and retry; a delay queue for users in quiet hours
tradeoffs: Names failures with conditions and a trade-off, such as: a crash after a claim and before the send loses that message, by the accepted rule; a provider outage is retried with backoff within the quota; a claim store that cannot be reached stops sending rather than risk duplicates; a summary that checks each requirement

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, deduplication in the database. Requirements: push handed over within 30 seconds; one SMS attempt only after a "not delivered" report and only if allowed then; rare misses after a crash accepted, duplicates not; offers only to opted-in users outside quiet hours, at most once, within 24 hours; quotas never exceeded. Estimates: 2,100 push requests per second with retries, under 5,000, with under 1 second in the queue; about 10 SMS per second expected; 2,100 inserts per second under 5,000; offers 6.3 million ÷ 500 ≈ 3.5 hours, 4.5 hours with an outage, ending by about 14:30 Pacific time, inside every user's daytime. API: notify(orderId, orderStatus, userId) from the order service. Data: preferences(user, channel, category), quiet hours and time zone; attempts(notification ID, channel) as primary key, with state claimed, sent, delivered or not delivered; the notification ID is (order, order status, user). High-level: order events → workers, which drop events older than 2 days and put one message on the push queue → push sender with a pacer at 5,000 per second; a delay queue holding each push's fallback check for 2 minutes; SMS sender with a pacer at 50 per second; offers queue → email sender with a pacer at 500 per second; each pacer counts retries. Deep dive: the push sender inserts (ID, push) as claimed, sends, then marks it sent; a redelivered event fails the insert and is skipped, so one push per order status. A crash after the claim and before the send leaves the attempt claimed; it is never resent, the accepted rare miss. After 2 minutes the fallback check reads the push report: only if it says not delivered and SMS is allowed at that moment, it inserts (ID, sms); a repeated check fails the insert, so at most one SMS, and a delivered push or a push that was never sent gets none. The email sender reads preferences and the user's local time just before each attempt, retries included; users in quiet hours go to a delay queue until 8:00; it inserts (offer week, user, email) and passes that key to the provider, so a retry after a crash, within the hour, is dropped by the provider. Attempts are kept 7 days, longer than the 2-day redelivery limit. Failures: a provider outage is retried with backoff through its pacer, so the quota holds and the offers still finish within 24 hours; if the database cannot be reached, senders stop rather than send unclaimed messages. Summary: each requirement is met. Trade-off: the database takes every claim.

Design B, deduplication in the in-memory store. Requirements and estimates as in Design A: 2,100 push requests per second, about 10 SMS per second, offers in about 3.5 hours, 4.5 with an outage, ending inside every user's daytime. API: the same notify call. Data: preferences in the database; attempt keys (notification ID, channel) in the in-memory store with a 7-day time limit, longer than the 2-day redelivery limit, acknowledged after the replica has them; workers drop older events, so an expired key is never needed. High-level: the same queues, senders, pacers and 2-minute delay queue for the fallback check. Deep dive: the push sender sets (ID, push) only if absent, about 2,100 per second against 100,000, and sends only if it was new; a crash after the set and before the send loses that push, by the accepted rule. The delayed check reads the push report: if not delivered and SMS is allowed at that moment, it sets (ID, sms) if absent and sends; a repeated check finds the key and sends nothing; a delivered push gets nothing. The email sender checks preferences and quiet hours just before each attempt, sets its key if absent, and passes the key to the email provider. Failures: if the store's main copy fails, the replica, which has every acknowledged key, takes over, so no key is forgotten; pacers keep every quota, retries included; if the store cannot be reached, senders stop. Summary: each requirement is met. Trade-off: keys live in a store that must be run with a replica, but the database takes no extra load.

assumptions: Push reports arrive within the stated 2 minutes
reference.design:
Requirements: push handed over within 30 seconds; one SMS attempt only after a "not delivered" report and only if SMS is allowed then; a rare miss after a crash between claim and send is accepted, a duplicate is not; offers only to users opted in at send time, outside 22:00 to 8:00 local time, at most once, all within 24 hours; quotas never exceeded, retries included.
Estimates: 2,000 alerts per second × 1.05 = 2,100 push requests against 5,000, with under 1 second in the queue; SMS about 2,000 × 1% × 50% = 10 per second expected against 50, bursts wait in the SMS queue; 2,100 claims per second against 5,000 inserts; offers 6.3 million ÷ 500 = 12,600 seconds, about 3.5 hours, 4.5 with a 1-hour outage, so from 10:00 Pacific time they end by about 14:30, inside every US user's daytime.
API: notify(orderId, orderStatus, userId). Data: preferences, quiet hours and time zone per user; attempts(notification ID, channel) as primary key with state claimed, sent, delivered or not delivered, where the notification ID is (order, order status, user).
Design and deep dive: workers drop events older than 2 days and queue one push per event; the push sender claims (ID, push) before sending, so a redelivered event is skipped, and a claimed attempt is never resent, the accepted rare miss. A fallback check 2 minutes later reads the push report and, only if it says not delivered and SMS is allowed at that moment, claims (ID, sms) and sends one SMS; a repeated check fails the claim. The email sender reads preferences and local time just before each attempt, holds users in quiet hours in a delay queue, claims its key and passes it to the provider, which drops a repeat for 24 hours. Attempts are kept 7 days, longer than the 2-day redelivery limit. Each provider has a pacer that counts retries.
Failures: provider outages are retried with backoff through the pacers; a store or database that cannot be reached stops new sends rather than risking duplicates. Summary: each requirement is met.
alternatives: Keys in an in-memory store with a replica and a time limit, instead of the database
Rejected: checking preferences when the offers batch is queued, because users who opt out before their email is sent would still get it
Rejected: sending the SMS at the same time as the push, because a delivered push would also get an SMS
